mainTopic: A husband's status regarding his wife's property (borrower, renter or buyer), מעילה with her הקדש, and a borrower's exemption when damage comes from normal work.
overview: The amud opens with רמי בר חמא's question: when a husband uses his wife's cow, is he a שואל or a שוכר? רבא objects that either way the wife works for him, so it is בבעלים and he is exempt. The גמרא therefore reframes the question twice, finally setting it in a case where the wife rented a cow from an outsider and then married. That version only works according to רבי יוסי, who holds a renter is not the owner. רבא answers that a husband is neither a borrower nor a renter but a לוקח, based on the תקנת אושא. רמי בר חמא then asks who commits מעילה when a husband acquires his wife's הקדש property. רבא first rules out the husband, the wife and the בית דין, and then concludes that the husband is liable once he actually spends it. Next, רב חלקיה and רבא establish that a borrower is exempt when an animal weakens or even dies from normal work. The amud ends with the cases of a broken borrowed ax: רבא requires witnesses, רב rules the borrower must pay for a good ax, and רב כהנא and רב אסי begin to challenge רב, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Is the husband a borrower or a renter?
steps.stepSummary: The closing words of רמי בר חמא's question about a husband using his wife's cow: is he treated as a שואל or as a שוכר?
steps.simpleTranslation: Is he a borrower, or is he a renter?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes stating רמי בר חמא's question. When a husband uses his wife's cow, which legal role does he have, borrower or renter?
steps.deeperAnalysis: A שואל and a שוכר carry different levels of responsibility for an animal in their care. So the question asks which set of rules applies to the husband. The next step will challenge whether this question even makes sense.

keyTerms.meaning: A borrower, who uses something for free
A renter, who pays to use something
Is he / is it considered

phrases.english: Is he a borrower, or is he a renter?

steps.triggerLanguage: שׁוֹאֵל הָוֵי, אוֹ שׂוֹכֵר הָוֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the question begun just before this section.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a husband using his wife's cow has the status of a borrower or of a renter.

steps.title: רבא: Either way he is exempt
steps.stepSummary: רבא says רמי בר חמא's sharp mind led him into a sharp mistake. Whether the husband is a borrower or a renter, his wife works for him, so it is a case of "with the owner" and he is exempt either way.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: the sharper the mind, the bigger the mistake. Whichever way you look at it, he is exempt. If he is a borrower, it is borrowing together with the owner. If he is a renter, it is renting together with the owner.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא rejects the question itself. He shows that the answer comes out the same no matter which side you pick.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תורה exempts someone who borrows an animal while its owner is working for him (בבעלים). The same exemption applies to renting. A wife is obligated to do household work for her husband, so she is "with him" in both cases, and it makes no difference whether he is a borrower or a renter.

keyTerms.meaning: The sharper the mind, the bigger the mistake
Whichever way you look at it
Borrowing while the owner is also working for you, which brings an exemption from paying
Renting while the owner is also working for you

steps.confusionAlert: רבא is not saying the husband is neither a borrower nor a renter. He is saying that whichever one he is, the "with the owner" exemption applies, so the question changes nothing.

phrases.english: Rava said: according to the sharpness is the error
phrases.notes: A gentle jab: a very sharp mind can also make a sharp mistake.

phrases.english: whichever way you look at it: if he is a borrower,
it is borrowing with the owner,
phrases.notes: His wife, the cow's owner, is working for him, because a wife does household work for her husband.

phrases.english: if he is a renter,
it is renting with the owner.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא, לְפוּם חוּרְפָּא שַׁבֶּשְׁתָּא – מָה נַפְשָׁךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the question in step 1 by showing it makes no practical difference.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The entire question as first framed
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Both sides of the question lead to the same exemption of בבעלים, because the wife works for her husband.

steps.title: The real question: he rented first, then married
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that רמי בר חמא was really asking about a man who rented a cow from a woman and only afterwards married her.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, when רמי בר חמא asked, it was about someone who rented a cow from her and then married her. Is he a borrower or a renter?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא saves רמי בר חמא's question by applying it to a different case. The rental started before the woman was working for him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the rental began without the owner, since she was not yet his wife. That means the בבעלים exemption does not clearly apply, and asking "borrower or renter" now has a real effect on the outcome.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather (a new explanation replaces the earlier one)
He was asking / he was unsure about
Who rented
And afterwards married her

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא כִּי קָמִיבַּעְיָא לֵיהּ לְרָמִי בַּר חָמָא:
phrases.english: Rather, when Rami bar Ḥama asked his question, it was:
where he rented a cow from her and then married her,
is he a borrower or is he a renter?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא כִּי קָמִיבַּעְיָא לֵיהּ לְרָמִי בַּר חָמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבא's rejection by moving the question to a case where it matters.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case behind the question
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The question was about any husband using his wife's cow, where בבעלים always applies.
steps.terutzMaskana: The question is about a rental that began before the marriage, without the owner, which then continued after the marriage.

steps.title: The two sides: does marriage replace the rental?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא spells out both sides. Either the husband becomes a borrower, and the new borrowing with the owner replaces the old rental, or he stays a renter and the original rental continues as it was.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is he a borrower, so that borrowing with the owner comes and cancels the rental that was without the owner? Or perhaps he is a renter, and the rental stays exactly as it was?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא lays out what each side of רמי בר חמא's question would mean. The next step challenges this way of framing the question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If marriage turns him into a borrower, a new arrangement "with the owner" begins and pushes out the old rental, so he is exempt. If he is still a renter, nothing new began. The old rental, made without the owner, continues, so the exemption does not apply.

keyTerms.meaning: Cancels / pushes out
Without the owner working with him
Or perhaps
It stays as it was

steps.whatToRemember: The question in its final form: when a rental made without the owner continues into a marriage, does the marriage start a new arrangement "with the owner" that cancels the old rental, or does the original rental just keep going?

phrases.english: Is he a borrower, so borrowing with the owner comes
and cancels the renting that was without the owner,
phrases.notes: The rental from before the wedding, when she was not yet working for him.

phrases.english: or perhaps he is a renter
and the renting stays as it was?

steps.triggerLanguage: שׁוֹאֵל הָוֵי וְאָתְיָא שְׁאֵלָה בִּבְעָלִים מַפְקְעָא שְׂכִירוּת שֶׁלֹּא בִּבְעָלִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the two possible outcomes of the reframed question in step 3.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether marriage creates a new borrowing "with the owner" that replaces the earlier rental, or whether the earlier rental without the owner simply continues.

steps.title: Why should only borrowing cancel the old rental?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the two sides laid out in step 4. If a new use 'with the owner' can cancel the old rental, it should do so whether the husband counts as a borrower or a renter.
steps.simpleTranslation: What's the difference? You said that if he is a borrower, the new borrowing with the owner cancels the old rental that was without the owner. But even if he is a renter, let the new rental with the owner come and cancel the old rental that was without the owner!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the way step 4 set up the question. The logic of 'the new arrangement cancels the old one' should work on both sides.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 4 said that only if he becomes a שואל does the new arrangement replace the old שכירות. The גמרא answers that a renting done בבעלים could replace the old rental just as well. Either way he ends up 'with the owner' and exempt, so the question falls apart.

keyTerms.meaning: What's the difference? A challenge to a distinction someone made.
Borrowing while the owner is working for you, which brings an exemption from paying.
Renting.
Cancels or pushes out.

phrases.english: But what is the difference?
That if he is a borrower,
the borrowing with the owner comes
and cancels the rental that was without the owner.
If he is a renter too,
let the rental with the owner come
and cancel the rental that was without the owner!
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets; the word in square brackets is the corrected wording, meaning 'cancel.'

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמַאי שְׁנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the two sides presented in step 4
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that only becoming a שואל would replace the original rental
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same 'new replaces old' reasoning applies to a new שכירות בבעלים, so both sides lead to an exemption and there is no real question.

steps.title: The real case: she rented the cow from someone else
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives a new version of the question. The woman rented a cow from an outside person and then got married.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, this is what רמי בר חמא was asking about: a case where she rented a cow from someone else, and afterward he married her.
steps.whatsHappening: Since the old version fell apart, the גמרא moves רמי בר חמא's question to a different case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the cow does not belong to the wife at all. She is only renting it from an outsider. So the question is whether the husband, who uses it once he marries her, counts as using it 'with the owner.'

keyTerms.meaning: Rather. It drops the earlier explanation and offers a new one.
Was asked; was a question someone could not resolve.
From the world, meaning from some outside person.
Married her.

steps.confusionAlert: Watch who did the renting. In step 3 the man rented from the woman. Now the woman rented from an outsider, and then the man married her.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא כִּי קָא מִיבַּעְיָא לְרָמֵי בַּר חָמָא:
phrases.english: Rather, when רמי בר חמא raised the question,
it was a case where she rented
a cow from someone else,
and afterward he married her.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא כִּי קָא מִיבַּעְיָא לְרָמֵי בַּר חָמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 5 by changing the case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The question was about a man who rented the wife's own cow and then married her.
steps.terutzMaskana: The question is about a cow the wife rented from an outsider before the marriage.

steps.title: According to רבנן there is no question
steps.stepSummary: According to רבנן, a renter is treated as the owner of the cow. So the husband is clearly borrowing with the owner, and there is nothing to ask.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to רבנן, who say that a borrower pays the renter, you should not ask. It is certainly a case of borrowing with the owner.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא narrows the question. It shows that one opinion leaves no room to ask at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבנן hold that when a renter lends out a cow, the borrower pays the renter, so the renter counts as the owner. That makes the wife the 'owner' here. The husband is using her cow while she works for him, which is plainly שאלה בבעלים.

keyTerms.meaning: According to the opinion of.
The Sages, the majority opinion.
The borrower pays the renter.
Don't ask; there is no question here.

phrases.english: And according to the Rabbis, who say:
a borrower pays the renter,
phrases.notes: This is the case on דף 35a. A renter lent the cow to a borrower, and then something happened to it.

phrases.english: you should not ask,
for it is certainly borrowing with the owner.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאַלִּיבָּא דְּרַבָּנַן דְּאָמְרִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the new version of the question from step 6
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבנן, the renter counts as the owner, so the husband's use is שאלה בבעלים and he is exempt.

steps.title: According to רבי יוסי: borrower or renter?
steps.stepSummary: The question only arises according to רבי יוסי, who holds that a renter is not the owner. Then we must ask whether the husband is a שואל or a שוכר.
steps.simpleTranslation: When should you ask? According to רבי יוסי, who says the cow goes back to its original owners. What is the husband then: a borrower or a renter?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא states the final, correct form of רמי בר חמא's question, according to רבי יוסי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוסי holds that the payment for the cow goes back to the first owner, so a renter is not treated as the owner. That means the husband's use is not automatically 'with the owner.' So we must ask whether he steps in as a renter like his wife, or counts as a borrower.

keyTerms.meaning: The original owners.
Borrower.
Renter.

steps.whatToRemember: רמי בר חמא's question is about a wife who rented a cow from an outsider before marrying. It only makes sense according to רבי יוסי, for whom a renter is not the owner.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows how a question that seems to stand alone can depend on an earlier מחלוקת. Here it is whether a renter counts as an owner.

phrases.english: When should you ask?
According to רבי יוסי, who says:
the cow should go back to its original owners,
phrases.notes: He means the payment for the cow goes to the person who first owned it, not to the renter.

phrases.aramaic: מַאי – שׁוֹאֵל הָוֵי, אוֹ שׂוֹכֵר הָוֵי?
phrases.english: what is he: a borrower, or a renter?

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי תִּיבְּעֵי לָךְ אַלִּיבָּא דְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the narrowing begun in step 7 by naming the opinion under which the question applies
steps.sheelahInformationSought: According to רבי יוסי, is a husband using a cow his wife rented from an outsider treated as a שואל or a שוכר?

steps.title: רבא: the husband is a buyer
steps.stepSummary: רבא rejects both options. The husband is neither a שואל nor a שוכר of his wife's property. He counts as a לוקח, and he learns this from רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: A husband is not a borrower and not a renter. He is a buyer. We learn this from רבי יוסי son of רבי חנינא.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the question from step 8. He says it was framed wrongly, because the husband is really a buyer of his wife's property.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 8 offered two choices, שואל or שוכר. רבא offers a third: the husband has real buyer-level rights in her property, not just the right to use it. He says the proof comes from רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא, which the גמרא quotes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: A buyer: someone who has acquired the property
A borrower, who uses an item for free
A renter, who pays to use an item

steps.confusionAlert: רבא is not choosing one of the two sides from step 8. He rejects both and gives a third category.

phrases.english: Rava said:
A husband is not a borrower
and he is not a renter;
rather, he is a buyer,
as we learn from Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Chanina.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: בַּעַל לָא שׁוֹאֵל הָוֵי וְלָא שׂוֹכֵר הָוֵי, אֶלָּא לוֹקֵחַ הָוֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the שאלה of step 8 by rejecting both of its options
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the husband is a שואל or a שוכר of his wife's property
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Neither. He is a לוקח, a buyer of her property.

steps.title: Proof from the enactment at Usha
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא reports the תקנה made at אושא. If a wife sold her נכסי מלוג while her husband was alive and then died, the husband can take the property back from the buyers.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי son of רבי חנינא said: At אושא they enacted that if a woman sold her נכסי מלוג while her husband was alive and then she died, the husband can take it back from the buyers.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the source behind רבא's claim that the husband is a buyer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The husband can take the property back from people who bought it from his wife. That means his own rights in it come first, as if he had bought it before them. Only a real buyer has that kind of power, so the husband counts as a לוקח.

keyTerms.meaning: A town where the חכמים made important enactments
They enacted a rabbinic rule (תקנה)
The wife's own property; the husband eats its produce but she keeps the property itself
Buyers

steps.whyThisMatters: The תקנת אושא is the standard source for the idea that a husband counts as a buyer of his wife's property.

phrases.english: For Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Chanina said:
In Usha they enacted:
A woman who sold some of her melog property
phrases.notes: These are her own fields and goods. She keeps ownership, but her husband gets to eat what they produce.

phrases.english: during her husband's lifetime, and then she died,
the husband takes it back from the buyers.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא: בְּאוּשָׁא הִתְקִינוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source that רבא pointed to in step 9
steps.raayaObject: רבא's claim that a husband is a לוקח of his wife's property
steps.raayaSupportSource: תקנת אושא as reported by רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא: the husband takes the property back from the buyers

steps.title: Who is liable for misuse of consecrated property?
steps.stepSummary: רמי בר חמא asks a new question. When a husband gains rights to his wife's property and some of it is הקדש, who is guilty of מעילה?
steps.simpleTranslation: רמי בר חמא asked: A husband who gains rights in his wife's property, when some of it is הקדש: who has committed מעילה?
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic starts here. רמי בר חמא asks who is responsible for מעילה when the husband acquires his wife's property and some of it belongs to the בית המקדש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Moving הקדש out of the בית המקדש's ownership is מעילה. Here the husband gains rights to the property, and the wife is the one who brought it into the marriage. It is unclear which of them, if either, is responsible.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked a question that is hard to settle
He committed מעילה, misusing consecrated property

phrases.english: Rami bar Chama asked:
A husband who gains rights in his wife's property,
who has committed misuse?
phrases.notes: The case is that some of her property is consecrated. Moving it out of the בית המקדש's hands counts as misuse.

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּעֵי רָמֵי בַּר חָמָא: בַּעַל בְּנִכְסֵי אִשְׁתּוֹ, מִי מָעַל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the idea that the husband acquires his wife's property and opens a new question about מעילה
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the husband or the wife is liable for מעילה when the husband acquires rights in her consecrated property

steps.title: The husband is not liable
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that no one is liable. He starts with the husband: he wants to acquire only permitted property, not forbidden הקדש.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Who would be liable? Should the husband be liable? He is happy to acquire the permitted property, but he is not happy to acquire the forbidden property.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא begins his answer by asking 'Who could be liable?' and then shows that the husband is not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מעילה needs someone who actually takes the הקדש for himself. The husband wants only the ordinary items, which he is allowed to use. He has no interest in acquiring הקדש, so his acquisition never reaches it.

keyTerms.meaning: Permitted things, here ordinary non-consecrated property
Forbidden things, here the consecrated property
It is pleasing to him; he wants it

phrases.english: Rava said: Who would be liable for misuse?
Should the husband be liable?
The permitted property, he is happy to acquire;
the forbidden property, he is not happy to acquire.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: מַאן לִימְעוֹל? לִימְעוֹל בַּעַל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering רמי בר חמא's question by ruling out the husband
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The husband is not liable, because he does not want to acquire the forbidden הקדש.

steps.title: The wife is not liable either
steps.stepSummary: The wife is not liable either. She does not even want her husband to acquire her permitted property, yet he acquires it anyway through the תקנה. So the transfer is not her doing.
steps.simpleTranslation: Should she be liable? Even the permitted property, she is not happy for him to acquire.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא continues his answer by ruling out the wife as well. The next step rules out the court too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The husband gains rights in her property because of the חכמים' rule, not because she agrees to it. Even with ordinary property, his rights take effect against her wishes. Since she is not the one transferring anything, she cannot be guilty of מעילה.

keyTerms.meaning: She
Also, even

phrases.english: Should she be liable for misuse?

phrases.aramaic: דְּהֶיתֵּרָא נָמֵי לָא נִיחָא לַהּ דְּלִיקְנֵי.
phrases.english: Even the permitted property, she is not happy for him to acquire.
phrases.notes: He gets her property anyway because of the חכמים' rule, so the transfer isn't her act.

steps.triggerLanguage: תִּימְעוֹל אִיהִי, דְּהֶיתֵּרָא נָמֵי לָא נִיחָא לַהּ דְּלִיקְנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רבא's answer by ruling out the wife after the husband; the court follows in step 14.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The wife is not liable, because the husband acquires her property through the תקנה even against her will, so the transfer is not her act.

steps.title: The court is not liable for מעילה either
steps.stepSummary: Maybe the בית דין is liable, since their תקנה gave the husband rights? No. The תקנה that makes a husband a לוקח only applies to permitted property, not to הקדש.
steps.simpleTranslation: Should the בית דין then be guilty of מעילה? No. When the חכמים made the תקנה that a husband counts as a buyer, they made it only for permitted property. They never made it for forbidden property.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes רבא's answer that no one is liable. It now rules out the last possible candidate, the בית דין that made the תקנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You might think the חכמים themselves moved the הקדש into the husband's hands through their תקנה. The answer is that the תקנה was limited from the start. It only made the husband a לוקח of permitted property, so it never moved any הקדש at all.

keyTerms.meaning: The rabbinic court, here meaning the חכמים who made the enactment
A rabbinic enactment, here the תקנה made at אושא
For permitted things, meaning ordinary non-holy property
For forbidden things, here meaning הקדש

phrases.english: Should the court be guilty of misusing הקדש?
phrases.notes: The idea is that the court's own enactment gave the husband his rights, so maybe they are the ones who moved the הקדש.

phrases.english: When the Rabbis made the enactment
and said that a husband counts as a buyer,
that was for permitted property;
for forbidden property, the Rabbis did not make the enactment.

steps.triggerLanguage: נִימְעֲלוּ בֵּית דִּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the list of people who might be liable. After the husband and the wife, the בית דין is also ruled out.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The בית דין is not liable, because the תקנה making the husband a לוקח never applied to הקדש.

steps.title: רבא's better answer: the husband is liable once he spends it
steps.stepSummary: רבא gives a new answer. The husband commits מעילה at the moment he actually spends the הקדש money. This is just like anyone who spends הקדש coins for ordinary use.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: the husband becomes guilty of מעילה when he spends the money. This is just like a person who spends הקדש coins for a non-holy purpose.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא replaces his earlier answer that no one is ever liable. He now says the husband does become liable, but only once he actually spends the money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The husband's legal rights did not create מעילה, because the תקנה did not cover הקדש. But spending הקדש money is itself an act of מעילה. So the husband becomes liable like any ordinary person who spends הקדש coins.

keyTerms.meaning: Committed מעילה, the misuse of הקדש property
When he spends it, literally 'when he takes it out'
Coins that belong to הקדש
Ordinary, non-holy use

steps.whatToRemember: The husband's rights under the תקנה do not make anyone guilty of מעילה. The husband only becomes liable when he actually spends the הקדש, like any other person who misuses הקדש.
steps.confusionAlert: This does not contradict step 14. Getting the property never caused מעילה, because the תקנה does not cover הקדש. The liability comes later, from the act of spending.

phrases.english: Rather, רבא said:
The husband is guilty of misuse once he spends it,

phrases.aramaic: מִידֵּי דְּהָוֵה אַמּוֹצִיא מְעוֹת הֶקְדֵּשׁ לְחוּלִּין.
phrases.english: just like one who spends הקדש coins for ordinary use.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רָבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The word אלא signals that רבא replaces his claim that no one is liable with a clearer rule.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The husband becomes liable for מעילה when he spends the הקדש, the same as anyone who spends הקדש coins for ordinary use.

steps.title: A borrowed animal grows thin from work
steps.stepSummary: A new question is raised. Someone borrowed an animal, and its flesh grew thin because of the work it did. What is the law?
steps.simpleTranslation: A question was asked: if the animal's flesh became weakened because of the work, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic about borrowing. It asks whether a borrower must pay when the borrowed animal grows thin from the work it did for him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The case is about a borrowed animal that was used for work and lost flesh because of that work. The question asks how a borrower is treated for this kind of damage.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was asked among the חכמים
Became thin or weakened
Because of the work it was doing

phrases.english: A question was asked:
If the flesh grew thin because of the work, what is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבַּעְיָא לְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the מעילה discussion behind and opens a new question about a borrower's liability.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is a borrower liable when the borrowed animal grows thin because of the work it did?

steps.title: רב חלקיה challenges the question itself
steps.stepSummary: רב חלקיה בריה דרב אויא points out that the question assumes something. It assumes that if the animal died from work, the borrower would be liable. He objects to that: the borrower can say he did not borrow the animal just to let it sit idle.
steps.simpleTranslation: One of the Rabbis, named רב חלקיה בריה דרב אויא, said to him: Your question implies that if the animal died from the work, the borrower would be liable. But let the borrower say: I didn't borrow it to stand it in a canopy!
steps.whatsHappening: A חכם attacks the starting assumption behind the question. He argues that the borrower should not be liable even if the animal died from ordinary work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question about thinning only makes sense if death from work would make the borrower liable. רב חלקיה rejects that idea. The owner lent the animal so it would be used. Harm that comes from that normal use should not be the borrower's fault.

keyTerms.meaning: By implication; it follows from what you said
A canopy, a sheltered place where something is kept safe and unused
I borrowed it

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the principle that harm from normal work may fall outside a borrower's liability. That idea shapes the rest of the discussion.

phrases.english: One of the Rabbis said to him,

phrases.aramaic: וְרַב חִלְקִיָּה בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אַוְיָא שְׁמֵיהּ:
phrases.english: and רב חלקיה son of רב אויא was his name:

phrases.aramaic: מִכְּלָל דְּכִי מֵתָה מֵחֲמַת מְלָאכָה מְחַיֵּיב?
phrases.english: This implies that if it died because of the work, he would be liable?
Let him say:
I didn't borrow it to keep it standing in a canopy!
phrases.notes: In other words: I borrowed it to use it, not to keep it safe and idle.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִכְּלָל דְּכִי מֵתָה מֵחֲמַת מְלָאכָה מְחַיֵּיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the hidden assumption behind the question in step 16.
steps.kashyaTarget: The assumption that a borrower is liable when the animal dies from work.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An animal is lent in order to be used. So damage or death from normal work should not make the borrower liable, and the borrower can claim he never borrowed it to keep it idle.

steps.title: רבא: even if the animal dies from normal work, the borrower is exempt
steps.stepSummary: רבא accepts the objection and restates the law. The borrower is exempt when the animal grows thin from work, and he is exempt even if it dies from work, because the owner lent it to be used.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: Of course a borrower is exempt if the animal grew thin from work. He is exempt even if it died from work. The borrower can say to the owner: I did not borrow it to let it rest under a canopy.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא drops the earlier question. He states plainly that work-related damage, even death, does not make the borrower pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier question assumed that death from work makes the borrower liable, and only asked about thinness. רב חלקיה's objection knocked out that assumption. So רבא concludes that if death from work is exempt, thinness from work is certainly exempt, and there is nothing left to ask.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not necessary to say. The easier case is obvious, and the harder case is also true.
The flesh grew thin, meaning the animal became weak or lean.
It died because of the work it did.
A canopy, a covered resting place.

steps.whatToRemember: A borrower is exempt when a borrowed animal dies or weakens from the normal work it was borrowed for (מתה מחמת מלאכה). The owner lent it to be used.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the basic rule of מתה מחמת מלאכה for a שואל. The ax cases that follow build on it.

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said:
It is not necessary to say that if its flesh grew thin
because of work, that he is exempt,
but even if it died because of work,
he is also exempt.
For he can say to him:
I did not borrow it to stand it under a canopy.
phrases.notes: He means: I did not borrow it to let it sit around resting. I borrowed it to work.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רָבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the objection of step 17 and replaces the question of step 16 with a clear ruling.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A borrower is exempt whether the animal grows thin or dies, as long as it happened through normal work.

steps.title: A borrowed ax breaks: רבא asks for witnesses
steps.stepSummary: A man borrowed an ax and it broke. רבא told him to bring witnesses that he used it in the normal way, and then he would be exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: A man borrowed an ax from his friend, and it broke. He came before רבא. רבא told him: Go bring witnesses that you did not misuse it, and you will be exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a real case that applies the rule from step 18 to a tool. רבא also adds that the borrower needs proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A tool breaking during normal use is like an animal dying from normal work, so the borrower is exempt. But the borrower must show he did not use it in an unusual way. That is why רבא asks for witnesses.

keyTerms.meaning: An ax.
It broke.
Witnesses.
You changed or deviated, meaning you used it differently from its normal use.

phrases.english: A certain man who borrowed
an ax from his friend, and it broke.
He came before Rava.
He said to him: Go bring witnesses
that you did not use it unusually, and be exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא גַּבְרָא דִּשְׁאֵיל נַרְגָּא מֵחַבְרֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the rule of מתה מחמת מלאכה to a tool, and adds the need for witnesses.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A borrower whose tool broke is exempt if he brings witnesses that he used it normally.

steps.title: What if there are no witnesses?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the law is when the borrower has no witnesses that he used the ax normally.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if there are no witnesses, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a follow-up question about רבא's ruling. It is setting up a source that will answer it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא's ruling only covered a borrower who has witnesses. Now the גמרא asks whether a borrower without proof must pay.

keyTerms.meaning: There is not, there are none.

phrases.english: And if there are no witnesses, what is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי לֵיכָּא סָהֲדִי מַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the case that רבא's ruling did not cover.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Must a borrower pay for a broken tool when he has no witnesses that he used it normally?

steps.title: רב ruled that the borrower must pay for a good ax
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a similar case. A borrowed ax broke, and רב told the borrower to pay the owner for a good, whole ax.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: A man borrowed an ax from his friend and it broke. He came before רב, and רב told him: Go pay him a good ax.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question with a case that רב judged. Since nothing is said about witnesses, it seems that without witnesses the borrower pays.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer comes from a real ruling, not from logic. רב made the borrower pay the full value of a good ax, so a borrower without proof is not exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: Pay, make good the loss.
Good, of proper quality.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
That a certain man who borrowed
an ax from his friend, and it broke,
came before Rav.
He said to him: Go pay him
a good ax.
phrases.notes: A good ax means a full, unbroken ax, not just the value of the broken pieces.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 20 with a ruling of רב.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Without witnesses, the borrower pays the full value of a good ax, as רב ruled.

steps.title: רב כהנא and רב אסי question רב
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא and רב אסי begin to respond to רב's ruling. Their words continue on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא and רב אסי said to רב:
steps.whatsHappening: This line only opens a challenge. The גמרא is setting up the next move, where רב כהנא and רב אסי question רב's ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב כהנא and רב אסי are about to question רב's ruling that the borrower must pay for a good ax. What exactly they say comes in the next lines.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ רַב כָּהֲנָא וְרַב אַסִּי לְרַב:
phrases.english: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi said to Rav:

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ רַב כָּהֲנָא וְרַב אַסִּי לְרַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a challenge to רב's ruling in step 21.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's ruling that the borrower must pay for a good ax.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The content of the challenge comes in the next lines. Here only the opening is given.
